# Saturation mutagenesis: DeepLoc + protGPS + TANGO + Deep-RBPPred on every RBP point mutant

Full missense saturation scan (every residue -> all 19 other amino
acids) across the 2,336 RBPs in `../rbp_filter/rbp_wt_list_with_go.tsv`,
scored for subcellular localization (DeepLoc2.1), condensate
partitioning (protGPS), aggregation propensity (TANGO), and RBP-ness
itself (Deep-RBPPred -- does a mutation predict to break the protein's
RNA-binding-protein classification?).

## Data source -- not regenerated by this repo

The mutant sequences themselves come from a labmate's (asharma)
independently-built file:

```
/u/project/kappel/asharma/RBP/saturation_mutagenesis/rbp_satmut_all.csv.gz
```

33,184,720 rows: 1,659,236 `is_wt=True` reference rows (one per residue
across all proteins) + 31,525,484 actual mutant rows (19 x 1,659,236,
confirming it's a complete per-residue scan). Columns include
`uniprot_accession, RBP_name, position, wt_aa, mut_aa, mutation, is_wt,
sequence` plus several MANE-transcript-mapping columns.

**This repo does not generate that file and has no copy of asharma's
own generation code.** Reproducing this specific step requires either
that exact file (checksum it if you copy it elsewhere) or asharma's
original script. Everything below starts from that file as a given
input.

## Pipeline

1. **`build_chunks_from_satmut_source.py`** -- streams the gzipped CSV,
   skips `is_wt=True` rows, writes FASTA chunks (header
   `>{uniprot_accession}|{RBP_name}|{mutation}`) of 140,000 sequences
   each to `satmut_chunks/chunk_NNNN.fasta`, plus a
   `satmut_manifest.tsv` (per-protein mutant counts). Produced 226
   chunks, 31,525,484 sequences written -- matches the source exactly.

2. **`submit_satmut_deeploc_array.sh`** -- DeepLoc2.1 array job, one
   task per chunk, 226 tasks. Each task writes to
   `satmut_deeploc_results/chunk_NNNN/` and ends with a hard
   correctness check (`exit 1` unless output row count >= input count),
   so a truncated/killed task shows up as a real job failure, not a
   half-written file that looks done.

3. **`submit_satmut_protgps_array.sh`** -- protGPS array job, same
   chunking, pinned to the lab's dedicated `kappel_gpu.q` node only.
   Same correctness-check pattern. protGPS is far cheaper per chunk
   (~27-32 min vs. DeepLoc's ~5.5-7h) so it isn't subject to the
   GPU-scheduling issues below.

4. **`submit_satmut_deeploc_retry.sh`** / **`submit_satmut_protgps_retry.sh`**
   -- backfill scripts for chunks that failed outright (see below). Edit
   the `CHUNKS=(...)` array and the `#$ -t 1-N` count to match, then
   `qsub` it.

5. **`submit_satmut_tango_array.sh`** + **`tango_predict_chunk.py`** --
   TANGO (aggregation propensity) array job, same 226 chunks, CPU-only
   (no GPU, so none of the account-wide GPU quota issues below apply).
   See "TANGO setup" below for the binary and environment details, and
   the resumability design that avoids needing a separate retry script
   for this one.

## Deep-RBPPred setup: a legacy Python 2 / TensorFlow 1.x environment

Deep-RBPPred (Yan et al.) predicts the probability that a sequence is
an RNA-binding protein at all, via a small CNN over 160 physical-
chemistry features. Obtained from the user as a local bundle
(`Deep-RBPPred.py`, a `feature` C++ binary + its `feature.cpp` source,
and two TensorFlow 1.x checkpoint pairs in `RBP_Model/` for the
"balance" and "unbalance" training variants) -- 2018-era code, not
distributed as a pip package.

**`feature` binary**: already Linux x86_64 (unlike TANGO's two separate
per-OS binaries), but the copy obtained needed a newer `libstdc++` than
Hoffman2's base system has. Recompiled directly from `feature.cpp` with
the system's own `g++` (`make`), which sidesteps the glibc++ version
mismatch entirely rather than chasing down a compatible shared library.

**Environment**: `Deep-RBPPred.py` requires Python 2.7 (print-statement
syntax) and TensorFlow 1.x's old `Saver`/`InteractiveSession` API
(matches the `.meta`/`.index`/`.data` checkpoint format) -- neither
exists in any other env in this repo. Building `deeprbppred` hit two
separate legacy-package problems worth recording:
- A fresh `conda create -n deeprbppred python=2.7` produced a
  non-functional `pip` (conda's own package metadata claimed it was
  installed; `python -m pip` disagreed). Fixed by bootstrapping via the
  official `https://bootstrap.pypa.io/pip/2.7/get-pip.py`, not by
  fighting conda's cache further.
- `pip install tensorflow==1.15.0` tried to build `grpcio` from source
  and failed (modern Cython 3.x is incompatible with grpcio's old
  `setup.py`). Fixed by pre-installing a pinned, wheel-available
  version (`pip install grpcio==1.27.2`) before installing tensorflow,
  so pip's resolver reused it instead of trying to build a newer one.

Exported to `../../environments/deeprbppred.yml` once working.

**Don't test on the login node.** The first end-to-end test crashed
with `std::system_error: Resource temporarily unavailable` -- not a
real bug, just TensorFlow's thread pool hitting the login node's
stricter resource limits. The same command succeeded immediately when
run as a trivial `qsub` job on a real compute node instead.

**Output pairing**: `Deep-RBPPred.py` prints one raw probability score
per line, in input order, with no sequence identity echoed back.
`deeprbppred_predict_chunk.sh` re-pairs each score with its FASTA
header (`mutation_id`) by position and asserts the counts match before
writing the final two-column TSV -- silently misaligning scores to the
wrong mutation if the two line counts ever diverged would be a much
worse failure than a job that errors out.

**Timing**: measured on real data (HNRNPA1 + RBM10's full mutant sets,
24,738 sequences): 48.2s total, ~15s of which is fixed TensorFlow
startup/model-load overhead, giving roughly ~1.95ms/sequence in steady
state. Confirmed at full chunk scale too: chunk_0001 (140,000
sequences) took 3m21s, matching that extrapolation closely. Far
cheaper than DeepLoc per sequence -- `submit_satmut_deeprbppred_array.sh`
uses `h_rt=1:00:00` (an ~18x safety margin over the observed per-chunk
time) and no `-q` restriction (plain CPU, like TANGO; no GPU quota
issues apply).

## TANGO setup: binary architecture and the resumable design

TANGO ships as two separate platform binaries, originally obtained
from the user as local files (`tango2_3_1`, a macOS Mach-O binary, and
`tango_x86_64_release`, a Linux ELF binary from the same distribution).
Only the Linux one runs on Hoffman2; it was copied to
`/u/home/d/ddcohn/tango_x86_64_release` and isn't itself checked into
this repo (it's a third-party binary, not something this pipeline
builds).

TANGO takes one sequence per invocation (`tango_bin <name> ct=N nt=N
ph=7.4 te=298 io=0.05 seq=<SEQUENCE>`), prints a one-line per-protein
summary to stdout (`AGG ... AMYLO ... TURN ... HELIX ... HELAGG ...
BETA ...`), and separately writes a large per-residue table to
`<name>.txt` that this pipeline doesn't need and deletes after each
call. Measured cost scales worse than linearly with sequence length
(~0.35s at 594 residues, ~7.3s at 8797 residues, the longest RBP in the
list) -- and since the source file groups mutants by protein, a single
140k-sequence chunk could in the worst case be dominated by one very
long protein's mutants, making naive per-chunk timing wildly uneven.

Rather than size `h_rt` for that worst case, `tango_predict_chunk.py`
is resumable at the sequence level: it checks which `mutation_id`s are
already present in the chunk's output TSV on startup and skips them,
writing (and flushing) each new result as it's computed. If a task
hits its wall-time limit partway through, resubmitting the exact same
task continues from where it left off -- no separate backfill script
or lost-chunk bookkeeping needed, unlike the DeepLoc/protGPS failure
modes below.

**That resumability turned out to be essential, not just a nice-to-have.**
The first full submission used `h_rt=8:00:00` -- copied from the
DeepLoc pattern without rechecking it against TANGO's own per-chunk
cost. At the real measured rate (~0.65-0.7s/sequence in practice,
somewhat higher than the isolated single-call benchmark above,
presumably filesystem/process overhead from 140,000 separate `tango_bin`
invocations per chunk), a full 140,000-sequence chunk needs **~25-27
hours** -- so literally every one of the 226 tasks hit the wall-time
kill, none finished. Checking real row counts (not queue state) caught
this immediately: 224/226 chunks incomplete, only ~29% of all rows
written after the first submission left the queue. Nothing was lost --
resubmitting the identical job continued every chunk from wherever it
had stopped -- but it's worth stating plainly: **this is a different
failure mode than the DeepLoc/protGPS cases below, where only a
minority of chunks failed.** Here, the resource request was wrong for
*every* chunk, not just a contention-unlucky few.

Fix: `h_rt=24:00:00`, the general shared CPU pool's hard maximum
(checked via `qconf -sq campus2.q`/`campus3.q`, the queues these tasks
actually land on) -- just under the ~25-27h estimated need, so a
single pass gets each chunk most of the way and a short follow-up
resubmission mops up whatever's left, rather than needing one job to
fit the entire runtime in one window.

Environment: no conda env needed for TANGO itself (the driver script
only uses the Python standard library), just `module load
miniforge/23.11.0` for a working `python3`.

## GPU scheduling: the account-wide cap and the queue-list fix

Submitting `submit_satmut_deeploc_array.sh` with no `-q` restriction
(the very first version) stalled at 2 concurrent tasks no matter what
`-tc` was set to. `qconf -srqs gpu` showed why: a hard per-account
resource-quota rule caps this account at **4 concurrent GPUs across the
entire general shared pool**, summed over every `gpu_*.q` queue
together -- not a per-queue or per-job limit.

Restricting the job to only the fast queues
(`-q gpu_l40s.q,gpu_a100.q,gpu_h100.q`) to try to speed up individual
chunks was a mistake: it dropped concurrency further (to 1), since none
of those queues had a free slot and the job could no longer fall back
to the slower `gpu_RTX2080Ti.q` it had been using. The fix that actually
works is SGE's **hard/soft queue split**, used in the two array scripts
above:

```
#$ -q gpu_RTX2080Ti.q,gpu_l40s.q,gpu_a100.q,gpu_h100.q   # hard: anywhere in this set
#$ -soft -q gpu_l40s.q,gpu_a100.q,gpu_h100.q              # soft: prefer these if free
```

This lets the scheduler grab a fast GPU when one's open, but never
blocks waiting for one -- it falls back to RTX2080Ti (which reliably
finishes a 140k-sequence chunk in ~5.5-7.2h) rather than sitting idle.

### Why the hard list excludes `gpu_smp.q` / `gpu_rh7.q`

An earlier attempt loosened the hard list to `*` (any queue on the
cluster) to maximize fallback options. Two tasks landed on
`gpu_smp.q`/`gpu_rh7.q` -- large, general-purpose, heavily shared
queues -- and both ran the full 8-hour `h_rt` wall-time limit without
finishing, then got SIGKILLed (`qacct` shows `failed=44` / "execd
enforced h_rt limit", `exit_status=137`). `qhost -F cuda` on those
nodes showed `hc:cuda=0` (no free GPU capacity) at dispatch time --
they're not dedicated GPU nodes, and heavy contention from unrelated
jobs made them far slower than RTX2080Ti for this workload. SGE does
**not** auto-retry a task killed this way; the chunk is just silently
dropped from the run unless you notice and backfill it yourself.

Net effect across the run so far: tasks landed on these two queues five
times before the hard list was narrowed back down to the four
known-good queues above. All five (chunks 5, 6, 9, 10, 11) had to be
resubmitted via `submit_satmut_deeploc_retry.sh`.

**Lesson:** when widening a hard queue list for fallback purposes,
widen it to specific named queues you've checked have real dedicated
GPU capacity (`qhost -h <host> -F cuda`, looking for consistent
non-zero `hc:cuda` capacity, not just a momentary free count) --
not to `*`.

### Verifying completion -- always by content, never by queue state alone

`qstat` showing a task as finished (or not in the queue) doesn't mean
it succeeded -- see the silent-failure case above. Verify every chunk
by comparing real row counts:

```bash
D=/u/project/kappel/ddcohn/protein_variant_effects/rbp_only
for c in $(ls $D/satmut_deeploc_results); do
  n_in=$(grep -c '^>' $D/satmut_chunks/${c}.fasta)
  f=$(ls $D/satmut_deeploc_results/$c/results_*.csv 2>/dev/null | head -1)
  n_out=$([ -n "$f" ] && echo $(($(wc -l < "$f") - 1)) || echo MISSING)
  [ "$n_out" != "$n_in" ] && echo "MISMATCH: $c in=$n_in out=$n_out"
done
```

And cross-check exit status directly against the scheduler's own
record rather than trusting a script's log output, since a process
killed by `h_rt` never reaches its own completion `echo`:

```bash
qacct -j <job_id> -t <task_id> | grep -E 'qname|failed|exit_status|ru_wallclock'
```

## Sharing a "dedicated" node with the general pool

`kappel_gpu.q` runs on a specific physical host that also has a general
-pool queue definition (`gpu_l40s.q`) on the same hardware. The lab's
RQS exemption gives this account rights to both GPUs on that box, but
if an unrelated user's job lands there first via the general queue,
only one GPU is actually free for us even though the node is nominally
"ours." Not a bug, not a permissions change -- just two queue
definitions sharing one host. Check `qhost -h <host> -F cuda` for the
real free count rather than assuming the dedicated queue's capacity is
exclusively available.

**We ended up contending with ourselves over this.** After adding
`gpu_l40s.q` to DeepLoc's fast-queue fallback list (see "GPU
scheduling" above), DeepLoc tasks started occasionally landing on
`gpu_l40s.q@g20` -- the *same physical node* as `kappel_gpu.q` --
since that queue spans multiple hosts and g20 is one of them. A
protGPS retry job then sat queued for most of a day with no obvious
cause; `qstat -f` eventually showed the two GPUs on g20 were held by
an outside user *and our own DeepLoc task*. Fixed by excluding g20
specifically from DeepLoc's `gpu_l40s.q` access -- explicit queue
instances (`gpu_l40s.q@g18,gpu_l40s.q@g19`) instead of the bare queue
name -- so DeepLoc keeps the rest of that pool without competing with
protGPS for the one node that's actually kappel's. Worth checking for
this kind of overlap any time two jobs' queue lists share a host,
even indirectly through a general-pool queue neither job names
explicitly as "the dedicated node."

**That exclusion was temporary, not a permanent policy** -- it only
existed to protect protGPS's retry while it was still running. Once
the full protGPS saturation-mutagenesis run finished and verified
clean (all 226 chunks), the exclusion was removed and
`submit_satmut_deeploc_array.sh` now includes `kappel_gpu.q` directly
in both its hard and soft queue lists again, same as the other fast
queues. If protGPS (or any other job meant to have priority on g20)
runs again while DeepLoc is still active, re-add the g18/g19-only
instance restriction above rather than assuming it's already in place.

**`kappel_gpu.q` is NOT exempt from the account-wide `cuda=4` cap.**
Fixing the node-sharing issue above didn't fully fix dispatch -- a
protGPS retry kept sitting queued even with `qhost -h g20 -F cuda`
showing a free GPU and `qalter -w v` confirming it was schedulable.
`qquota -u ddcohn` was the thing that actually explained it:
`gpu/10  cuda=4/4  users ddcohn  hosts g*` -- a blanket account-wide
rule matching every GPU host by the `g*` pattern, kappel_gpu.q's `g20`
included. DeepLoc was simply holding all 4 of the account's GPU slots
on the general pool (confirmed via `qstat -u ddcohn | grep 14964933`),
so there was zero quota headroom left for protGPS to claim *any*
GPU, anywhere, regardless of a physically free slot on g20. The
earlier-RQS-investigation belief that kappel's exemption
(`limit users !@kappel hosts @kappel_gpu to cuda=1`, which only
exempts kappel members from a *different*, narrower 1-GPU cap) made
`kappel_gpu.q` sit outside the general 4-GPU accounting entirely was
wrong -- it doesn't. Fix in the moment: `qalter -tc 3 14964933` to
free a slot from DeepLoc's quota share, restored to unthrottled
(`qalter -tc 0`) once protGPS cleared. If this keeps recurring, the
real fix is deciding a standing concurrency split between the two
jobs up front rather than firefighting it live each time.

## protGPS also hit a wall-time kill, same lesson as DeepLoc's

Even though protGPS normally finishes a 140k-sequence chunk in ~27-32
min, 5 of 226 chunks (0077, 0113, 0147, 0174, 0183) silently landed
short -- `qstat` showed the job had left the queue entirely, and all
226 output files existed, but comparing real row counts against input
counts caught 5 truncated files (e.g. chunk_0183: 94,493 of 140,000
expected rows). `qacct` confirmed the same signature as the DeepLoc
failures: `failed=44`, `exit_status=137`, wall time pinned at exactly
7200s -- the original `h_rt=2:00:00` was too tight for a handful of
chunks that landed during heavier-than-usual contention on the shared
`g20` node. The submit script's `h_rt` is now `6:00:00`.

`protgps_predict_scale.py` opens its output file in `"w"` mode (not
append), so unlike the DeepLoc case, a clean resubmit of a failed task
safely overwrites the partial file rather than needing any dedup
logic -- see `submit_satmut_protgps_retry.sh`.

**Lesson, stated generally:** "the job left the queue" and "all output
files exist" are both necessary but not sufficient. The only real
completion check is comparing actual row/sequence counts, every time,
for every tool -- this is now the third time in this pipeline alone
(DeepLoc's `gpu_smp.q`/`gpu_rh7.q` failures, TANGO's resumable design
was built specifically to preempt this, and now protGPS) that a
wall-time kill produced a file that looked done from the outside.
